messages.body_plain:
OK, thanks. How do we disable the limit of 10 dimensions for saving proposal covariance histories?

Also, any suggestions on how to go about identifying reasonable proposal covariances? All I can think of doing is running the model for a short bit and then saving the proposal covariances, but then I’m not sure I’m doing anything more than the automated algorithm for determining the covariance. Are there any good references you can suggest that describe approaches for tuning block samplers?

Quresh S. Latif
Research Scientist
Bird Conservancy of the Rockies
Phone: (970) 482-1707 ext. 15
www.birdconservancy.org <http://www.birdconservancy.org/>

From: Daniel Turek <danie...@gmail.com>
Sent: Tuesday, June 20, 2023 6:45 PM
To: Quresh Latif <quresh...@birdconservancy.org>
Cc: nimble-users <nimble...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: Re: Improving MCMC convergence

Quresh, thanks for the message, and it's great that you're digging into these aspects of the samplers.  Just a few comments.

You could easily work around the limit of 10 dimensions (parameters) for saved proposal covariance histories from the RW_block sampler, and have this history be saved for larger groups of parameters if you wish.  Just be aware of how the memory usage would scale, as d*d*nAdapt, where d is the dimension of the parameter block, and nAdapt is the number of adaptation phases of the RW_block sampler.

No, I don't agree that "in most cases it probably won't be all that helpful to look at or tweak the covariances in order to optimize mixing?".  The restriction of saving proposal covariance history only for <= 10 dimensional blocks is only for memory-related concerns.  And it's true that the RW_block sampler will likely not operate with any practical efficiency (that is: it will have very low acceptance rate) when *all* of the following are true: (i) operating in high dimensions, (ii) the dimensions are on quite different scales and/or exhibit high correlations between dimensions, and (iii) you do not provide an accurate and informative starting value for the proposal covariance.  However, this situation can be avoided by provided a reasonably accurate starting value for the proposal covariance, and I would also suggest using a small initial "scale" value (subject to tuning, but certainly less than 1).  You can also further encourage efficiency of the RW_block sampler using the "tries" argument, by providing an integer value greater than 1, which will afford the sampler multiple propose-accept/reject cycles for each MCMC iteration.  Following these suggestions, the RW_block sampler could in theory operate quite well even in high dimensions - while being less computationally expensive than the AFSS sampler.  All that said, joint sampling in high dimensional space is generally a difficult problem.

Regarding the final part of your question: no, even if all dimensions are scaled similarly, for high dimensional sampling it will still be extremely helpful to provide an informative (and accurate) starting value for the proposal covariance, assuming there's nontrivial correlation between the various dimensions.

I hope this helps.  Cheers,

Daniel

Specifically, length-n proposal vectors are generated as MVN(0, cov = Sigma), where Sigma = propCov * scale^2, where Sigma is covariance matrix used to generate the proposed transitions.  During the course of MCMC sampling, the 'propCov' matrix adapts towards the empirical covariance of the posterior samples (which is used to approximate the true covariance of the target dimensions of the posterior distribution).  The 'scale' variable adapts independently, in order to achieve the (theoretically) optimal acceptance rate for the RW_block sampler.  If the acceptance rate is too low, for example, then the 'scale' value will adaptively decrease, to generate smaller (closer to the origin in R^n) proposal vectors, which are more likely to be accepted.
> >
> >
> >
> > 2. In that example, the 'scale' could just as well be set also.  But, in the example, we provide an informed initial value for the 'propCov' matrix, then rely on the automatic adaptation of the 'scale' variable.  There is no good reason that the 'scale' was not set, as well.
> >
> >
> >
> > 2b. If by "fix the tuning" you mean set the sampler tuning parameters to immutable values, then you should also set adaptive = FALSE (in addition to providing values for 'propCov' and 'scale').  If you want to provide a fixed covariance structure for proposals, but allow 'scale' to self-adapt to achieve the (theoretically) optimal acceptance rate, then you should set adaptScaleOnly = TRUE (in addition to providing a value for 'propCov').  Alternatively, you can allow these variables to adapt on their own (leaving the default values of adaptive = TRUE and adaptScaleOnly = FALSE), while also providing starting values for 'propCov' and/or 'scale', as you desire.  Nimble is here to meet your needs.
> >
> >
> >
> > 3. No, assigning two samplers (say A and B) to the same parameter (say, theta) does not operate as two chains.  It's one chain, where the chain is generated as:
> >
> > (a) sampler A acts on theta, and may modify the value of theta
> >
> > (b) sampler B acts on theta, and may further modify the value of theta
> >
> > (c) record the current value of theta as the next value in the (single) chain of samples
> >
> > (d) goto (a) above
> >
> >
> >
> > To see all the samplers that are operating, printed in the order in which they'll operate, between each successive sample that is recorded, don't forget about our old friend:
> >
> >
> >
> > conf$printSamplers()
> >
> >
> >
> > Cheers,
> >
> > Daniel

> > > > > > > > > Sometimes the list of samplers operating on a model represents misplaced computational costs.  A categorical sampler for a node with many categories can be inefficient, and that node may not be a limitation on mixing, so it can work well to use a faster sampler.  Sometimes multiple nodes share identical or nearly identical dependencies (other nodes that depend on them).  This means that the same computational effort is involved in sampling them, and for this reason it can make sense to sample them jointly, such as with RW_block.  Sometimes we can identify parts of a model that can be re-written using nimbleFunctions to provide new functions or distributions in the model.  New functions can combine multiple steps into single steps, reducing the size of the model, which can improve efficiency.  New distributions can be useful to analytically sum or integrate over latent states when it is simple to do so.  The zero-inflated Poisson example on our web site is a simple case. messages.subject: Re: Improving MCMC convergence
messages.body_plain:
Although somewhat crude, the most straightforward approach is to copy the sampler code (copied directly from line 324 of  MCMC_samplers.R <https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/blob/ebfd5a2b730986c66f52a3a6c27dfcea55bde21b/packages/nimble/R/MCMC_samplers.R#L324>), remove this check that d<=10, and define a new sampler (below called sampler_RW_block2).  Then, using conf$removeSamplers() and conf$addSampler(), use this custom sampler_RW_block2 in place of the original RW_block samplers.

Your approach is reasonable, as it will give the sampler progressively better and better starting structures for the covariance.  I'm sorry but I don't have other suggestions or references for this process; perhaps others on the list will have better ideas.

Modified sampler code is below.

sampler_RW_block2 <- nimbleFunction(
    name = 'sampler_RW_block2',
    contains = sampler_BASE,
    setup = function(model, mvSaved, target, control) {
        ## control list extraction
        adaptive            <- extractControlElement(control, 'adaptive',            TRUE)
        adaptScaleOnly      <- extractControlElement(control, 'adaptScaleOnly',      FALSE)
        adaptInterval       <- extractControlElement(control, 'adaptInterval',       200)
        adaptFactorExponent <- extractControlElement(control, 'adaptFactorExponent', 0.8)
        scale               <- extractControlElement(control, 'scale',               1)
        propCov             <- extractControlElement(control, 'propCov',             'identity')
        tries               <- extractControlElement(control, 'tries',               1)
        ## node list generation
        targetAsScalar <- model$expandNodeNames(target, returnScalarComponents = TRUE)
        ccList <- mcmc_determineCalcAndCopyNodes(model, target)
        calcNodes <- ccList$calcNodes; copyNodesDeterm <- ccList$copyNodesDeterm; copyNodesStoch <- ccList$copyNodesStoch   # not used: calcNodesNoSelf
        finalTargetIndex <- max(match(model$expandNodeNames(target), calcNodes))
        if(!is.integer(finalTargetIndex) | length(finalTargetIndex) != 1 | is.na <http://is.na>(finalTargetIndex[1]))   stop('problem with target node in RW_block sampler')
        calcNodesProposalStage <- calcNodes[1:finalTargetIndex]
        calcNodesDepStage <- calcNodes[-(1:finalTargetIndex)]
        ## numeric value generation
        scaleOriginal <- scale
        timesRan      <- 0
        timesAccepted <- 0
        timesAdapted  <- 0
        d <- length(targetAsScalar)
        scaleHistory <- c(0, 0)                                                  ## scaleHistory
        acceptanceHistory  <- c(0, 0)                                            ## scaleHistory
        propCovHistory <- array(0, c(2,d,d))                                     ## scaleHistory
        saveMCMChistory <- if(nimbleOptions('MCMCsaveHistory')) TRUE else FALSE
        if(is.character(propCov) && propCov == 'identity')     propCov <- diag(d)
        propCovOriginal <- propCov
        chol_propCov <- chol(propCov)
        chol_propCov_scale <- scale * chol_propCov
        empirSamp <- matrix(0, nrow=adaptInterval, ncol=d)
        ## nested function and function list definitions
        targetNodesAsScalar <- model$expandNodeNames(target, returnScalarComponents = TRUE)
        my_calcAdaptationFactor <- calcAdaptationFactor(d, adaptFactorExponent)
        ## checks
        if(!inherits(propCov, 'matrix'))        stop('propCov must be a matrix\n')
        if(!inherits(propCov[1,1], 'numeric'))  stop('propCov matrix must be numeric\n')
        if(!all(dim(propCov) == d))             stop('propCov matrix must have dimension ', d, 'x', d, '\n')
        if(!isSymmetric(propCov))               stop('propCov matrix must be symmetric')
    },
    run = function() {
        for(i in 1:tries) {
            propValueVector <- generateProposalVector()
            values(model, targetNodesAsScalar) <<- propValueVector
            lpD <- model$calculateDiff(calcNodesProposalStage)
            if(lpD == -Inf) {
                jump <- FALSE
                nimCopy(from = mvSaved, to = model,   row = 1, nodes = calcNodesProposalStage, logProb = TRUE)
            } else {
                lpD <- lpD + model$calculateDiff(calcNodesDepStage)
                jump <- decide(lpD)
                if(jump) {
                    ##model$calculate(calcNodesPPomitted)
                    nimCopy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row = 1, nodes = calcNodesProposalStage, logProb = TRUE)
                    nimCopy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row = 1, nodes = copyNodesDeterm, logProb = FALSE)
                    nimCopy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row = 1, nodes = copyNodesStoch, logProbOnly = TRUE)
                } else {
                    nimCopy(from = mvSaved, to = model, row = 1, nodes = calcNodesProposalStage, logProb = TRUE)
                    nimCopy(from = mvSaved, to = model, row = 1, nodes = copyNodesDeterm, logProb = FALSE)
                    nimCopy(from = mvSaved, to = model, row = 1, nodes = copyNodesStoch, logProbOnly = TRUE)
                }
            }
            if(adaptive)     adaptiveProcedure(jump)
        }
    },
    methods = list(
        generateProposalVector = function() {
            propValueVector <- rmnorm_chol(1, values(model,target), chol_propCov_scale, 0)  ## last argument specifies prec_param = FALSE
            returnType(double(1))
            return(propValueVector)
        },
        adaptiveProcedure = function(jump = logical()) {
            timesRan <<- timesRan + 1
            if(jump)     timesAccepted <<- timesAccepted + 1
            if(!adaptScaleOnly)     empirSamp[timesRan, 1:d] <<- values(model, target)
            if(timesRan %% adaptInterval == 0) {
                acceptanceRate <- timesAccepted / timesRan
                timesAdapted <<- timesAdapted + 1
                if(saveMCMChistory) {
                    setSize(scaleHistory, timesAdapted)                 ## scaleHistory
                    scaleHistory[timesAdapted] <<- scale                ## scaleHistory
                    setSize(acceptanceHistory, timesAdapted)            ## scaleHistory
                    acceptanceHistory[timesAdapted] <<- acceptanceRate  ## scaleHistory
                    propCovTemp <- propCovHistory                                           ## scaleHistory
                    setSize(propCovHistory, timesAdapted, d, d)                             ## scaleHistory
                    if(timesAdapted > 1)                                                    ## scaleHistory
                        for(iTA in 1:(timesAdapted-1))                                      ## scaleHistory
                            propCovHistory[iTA, 1:d, 1:d] <<- propCovTemp[iTA, 1:d, 1:d]    ## scaleHistory
                    propCovHistory[timesAdapted, 1:d, 1:d] <<- propCov[1:d, 1:d]            ## scaleHistory
                }
                adaptFactor <- my_calcAdaptationFactor$run(acceptanceRate)
                scale <<- scale * adaptFactor
                ## calculate empirical covariance, and adapt proposal covariance
                if(!adaptScaleOnly) {
                    gamma1 <- my_calcAdaptationFactor$getGamma1()
                    for(i in 1:d)     empirSamp[, i] <<- empirSamp[, i] - mean(empirSamp[, i])
                    empirCov <- (t(empirSamp) %*% empirSamp) / (timesRan-1)
                    propCov <<- propCov + gamma1 * (empirCov - propCov)
                    chol_propCov <<- chol(propCov)
                }
                chol_propCov_scale <<- chol_propCov * scale
                timesRan <<- 0
                timesAccepted <<- 0
            }
        },
        setScale = function(newScale = double()) {
            scale         <<- newScale
            scaleOriginal <<- newScale
            chol_propCov_scale <<- chol_propCov * scale
        },
        setPropCov = function(newPropCov = double(2)) {
            propCov         <<- newPropCov
            propCovOriginal <<- newPropCov
            chol_propCov <<- chol(propCov)
            chol_propCov_scale <<- chol_propCov * scale
        },
        getScaleHistory = function() {  ## scaleHistory
            if(!saveMCMChistory)   print("Please set 'nimbleOptions(MCMCsaveHistory = TRUE)' before building the MCMC.")
            returnType(double(1))
            return(scaleHistory)
        },
        getAcceptanceHistory = function() {  ## scaleHistory
            returnType(double(1))
            if(!saveMCMChistory)   print("Please set 'nimbleOptions(MCMCsaveHistory = TRUE)' before building the MCMC.")
            return(acceptanceHistory)
        },
        getPropCovHistory = function() { ## scaleHistory
            if(!saveMCMChistory)   print("Please set 'nimbleOptions(MCMCsaveHistory = TRUE)' before building the MCMC and note that to reduce memory use we only save the proposal covariance history for parameter vectors of length infinity or less.")
            returnType(double(3))
            return(propCovHistory)
        },
        reset = function() {
            scale   <<- scaleOriginal
            propCov <<- propCovOriginal
            chol_propCov <<- chol(propCov)
            chol_propCov_scale <<- chol_propCov * scale
            timesRan      <<- 0
            timesAccepted <<- 0
            timesAdapted  <<- 0
            if(saveMCMChistory) {
                scaleHistory  <<- c(0, 0)    ## scaleHistory
                acceptanceHistory  <<- c(0, 0)
                propCovHistory <<- nimArray(0, dim = c(2,d,d))
            }
            my_calcAdaptationFactor$reset()
        }
    )
)

> You could easily work around the limit of 10 dimensions (parameters) for saved proposal covariance histories from the RW_block sampler, and have this history be saved for larger groups of parameters if you wish.  Just be aware of how the memory usage would scale, as d*d*nAdapt, where d is the dimension of the parameter block, and nAdapt is the number of adaptation phases of the RW_block sampler.

> No, I don't agree that "in most cases it probably won't be all that helpful to look at or tweak the covariances in order to optimize mixing?".  The restriction of saving proposal covariance history only for <= 10 dimensional blocks is only for memory-related concerns.  And it's true that the RW_block sampler will likely not operate with any practical efficiency (that is: it will have very low acceptance rate) when *all* of the following are true: (i) operating in high dimensions, (ii) the dimensions are on quite different scales and/or exhibit high correlations between dimensions, and (iii) you do not provide an accurate and informative starting value for the proposal covariance.  However, this situation can be avoided by provided a reasonably accurate starting value for the proposal covariance, and I would also suggest using a small initial "scale" value (subject to tuning, but certainly less than 1).  You can also further encourage efficiency of the RW_block sampler using the "tries" argument, by providing an integer value greater than 1, which will afford the sampler multiple propose-accept/reject cycles for each MCMC iteration.  Following these suggestions, the RW_block sampler could in theory operate quite well even in high dimensions - while being less computationally expensive than the AFSS sampler.  All that said, joint sampling in high dimensional space is generally a difficult problem.
>
>
>
> Regarding the final part of your question: no, even if all dimensions are scaled similarly, for high dimensional sampling it will still be extremely helpful to provide an informative (and accurate) starting value for the proposal covariance, assuming there's nontrivial correlation between the various dimensions.

> > >
> > >
> > > For RW_block samplers, the (scalar) 'scale' and the (matrix) 'propCov' tuning parameters are used together to generate new MH proposals.  Specifically, length-n proposal vectors are generated as MVN(0, cov = Sigma), where Sigma = propCov * scale^2, where Sigma is covariance matrix used to generate the proposed transitions.  During the course of MCMC sampling, the 'propCov' matrix adapts towards the empirical covariance of the posterior samples (which is used to approximate the true covariance of the target dimensions of the posterior distribution).  The 'scale' variable adapts independently, in order to achieve the (theoretically) optimal acceptance rate for the RW_block sampler.  If the acceptance rate is too low, for example, then the 'scale' value will adaptively decrease, to generate smaller (closer to the origin in R^n) proposal vectors, which are more likely to be accepted.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > 2. In that example, the 'scale' could just as well be set also.  But, in the example, we provide an informed initial value for the 'propCov' matrix, then rely on the automatic adaptation of the 'scale' variable.  There is no good reason that the 'scale' was not set, as well.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > 2b. If by "fix the tuning" you mean set the sampler tuning parameters to immutable values, then you should also set adaptive = FALSE (in addition to providing values for 'propCov' and 'scale').  If you want to provide a fixed covariance structure for proposals, but allow 'scale' to self-adapt to achieve the (theoretically) optimal acceptance rate, then you should set adaptScaleOnly = TRUE (in addition to providing a value for 'propCov').  Alternatively, you can allow these variables to adapt on their own (leaving the default values of adaptive = TRUE and adaptScaleOnly = FALSE), while also providing starting values for 'propCov' and/or 'scale', as you desire.  Nimble is here to meet your needs.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > 3. No, assigning two samplers (say A and B) to the same parameter (say, theta) does not operate as two chains.  It's one chain, where the chain is generated as:
> > >
> > > (a) sampler A acts on theta, and may modify the value of theta
> > >
> > > (b) sampler B acts on theta, and may further modify the value of theta
> > >
> > > (c) record the current value of theta as the next value in the (single) chain of samples
> > >
> > > (d) goto (a) above
> > >
> > >

> > > > > > > > > > Sometimes the list of samplers operating on a model represents misplaced computational costs.  A categorical sampler for a node with many categories can be inefficient, and that node may not be a limitation on mixing, so it can work well to use a faster sampler.  Sometimes multiple nodes share identical or nearly identical dependencies (other nodes that depend on them).  This means that the same computational effort is involved in sampling them, and for this reason it can make sense to sample them jointly, such as with RW_block.  Sometimes we can identify parts of a model that can be re-written using nimbleFunctions to provide new functions or distributions in the model.  New functions can combine multiple steps into single steps, reducing the size of the model, which can improve efficiency.  New distributions can be useful to analytically sum or integrate over latent states when it is simple to do so.  The zero-inflated Poisson example on our web site is a simple case.  More complicated cases of doing this for capture-recapture and hidden Markov models are given in Turek et al. (2016; Environ Ecol Stat (2016) 23: 549. https://link.edgepilot.com/s/53661c95/X7avF18thkyInmDB4XXrbA?u=https://doi.org/10.1007/s10651-016-0353-z).  Sometimes changing the parameterization of a model (e.g. from non-centered to centered random effects) or centering explanatory variables can lead to improved mixing.

messages.subject: RE: Improving MCMC convergence
messages.body_plain:
Awesome, thank you!

I imagine you might be dreading this question, but would it make sense to have an option built in to toggle the d<=10 limit off, possibly along with a warning that this should only be toggled off for small preliminary runs to avoid overloading memory? Totally understandable if this level of customization is outside the scope of your development plan for NIMBLE, considering that you allow for users to supply their own samplers.

Quresh S. Latif
Research Scientist
Bird Conservancy of the Rockies
Phone: (970) 482-1707 ext. 15
www.birdconservancy.org <http://www.birdconservancy.org/>

From: Daniel Turek <danie...@gmail.com>
Sent: Wednesday, June 21, 2023 12:00 PM
To: Quresh Latif <quresh...@birdconservancy.org>
Cc: nimble-users <nimble...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: Re: Improving MCMC convergence

Although somewhat crude, the most straightforward approach is to copy the sampler code (copied directly from line 324 of  MCMC_samplers.R <https://link.edgepilot.com/s/ed07429d/NqiQF_cUIU6PlBqxKnNx0w?u=https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/blob/ebfd5a2b730986c66f52a3a6c27dfcea55bde21b/packages/nimble/R/MCMC_samplers.R%23L324>), remove this check that d<=10, and define a new sampler (below called sampler_RW_block2).  Then, using conf$removeSamplers() and conf$addSampler(), use this custom sampler_RW_block2 in place of the original RW_block samplers.

Your approach is reasonable, as it will give the sampler progressively better and better starting structures for the covariance.  I'm sorry but I don't have other suggestions or references for this process; perhaps others on the list will have better ideas.

Modified sampler code is below.

sampler_RW_block2 <- nimbleFunction(
    name = 'sampler_RW_block2',
    contains = sampler_BASE,
    setup = function(model, mvSaved, target, control) {
        ## control list extraction
        adaptive            <- extractControlElement(control, 'adaptive',            TRUE)
        adaptScaleOnly      <- extractControlElement(control, 'adaptScaleOnly',      FALSE)
        adaptInterval       <- extractControlElement(control, 'adaptInterval',       200)
        adaptFactorExponent <- extractControlElement(control, 'adaptFactorExponent', 0.8)
        scale               <- extractControlElement(control, 'scale',               1)
        propCov             <- extractControlElement(control, 'propCov',             'identity')
        tries               <- extractControlElement(control, 'tries',               1)
        ## node list generation
        targetAsScalar <- model$expandNodeNames(target, returnScalarComponents = TRUE)
        ccList <- mcmc_determineCalcAndCopyNodes(model, target)
        calcNodes <- ccList$calcNodes; copyNodesDeterm <- ccList$copyNodesDeterm; copyNodesStoch <- ccList$copyNodesStoch   # not used: calcNodesNoSelf
        finalTargetIndex <- max(match(model$expandNodeNames(target), calcNodes))
        if(!is.integer(finalTargetIndex) | length(finalTargetIndex) != 1 | is.na <https://link.edgepilot.com/s/a6ee79b4/QrioaHM7aUCTUyeDjm0G_A?u=http://is.na/>(finalTargetIndex[1]))   stop('problem with target node in RW_block sampler')
        calcNodesProposalStage <- calcNodes[1:finalTargetIndex]
        calcNodesDepStage <- calcNodes[-(1:finalTargetIndex)]
        ## numeric value generation
        scaleOriginal <- scale
        timesRan      <- 0
        timesAccepted <- 0
        timesAdapted  <- 0
        d <- length(targetAsScalar)
        scaleHistory <- c(0, 0)                                                  ## scaleHistory
        acceptanceHistory  <- c(0, 0)                                            ## scaleHistory
        propCovHistory <- array(0, c(2,d,d))                                     ## scaleHistory
        saveMCMChistory <- if(nimbleOptions('MCMCsaveHistory')) TRUE else FALSE
        if(is.character(propCov) && propCov == 'identity')     propCov <- diag(d)
        propCovOriginal <- propCov
        chol_propCov <- chol(propCov)
        chol_propCov_scale <- scale * chol_propCov
        empirSamp <- matrix(0, nrow=adaptInterval, ncol=d)
        ## nested function and function list definitions
        targetNodesAsScalar <- model$expandNodeNames(target, returnScalarComponents = TRUE)
        my_calcAdaptationFactor <- calcAdaptationFactor(d, adaptFactorExponent)
        ## checks
        if(!inherits(propCov, 'matrix'))        stop('propCov must be a matrix\n')
        if(!inherits(propCov[1,1], 'numeric'))  stop('propCov matrix must be numeric\n')
        if(!all(dim(propCov) == d))             stop('propCov matrix must have dimension ', d, 'x', d, '\n')
        if(!isSymmetric(propCov))               stop('propCov matrix must be symmetric')
    },
    run = function() {
        for(i in 1:tries) {
            propValueVector <- generateProposalVector()
            values(model, targetNodesAsScalar) <<- propValueVector
            lpD <- model$calculateDiff(calcNodesProposalStage)
            if(lpD == -Inf) {
                jump <- FALSE
                nimCopy(from = mvSaved, to = model,   row = 1, nodes = calcNodesProposalStage, logProb = TRUE)
            } else {
                lpD <- lpD + model$calculateDiff(calcNodesDepStage)
                jump <- decide(lpD)
                if(jump) {
                    ##model$calculate(calcNodesPPomitted)
                    nimCopy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row = 1, nodes = calcNodesProposalStage, logProb = TRUE)
                    nimCopy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row = 1, nodes = copyNodesDeterm, logProb = FALSE)
                    nimCopy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row = 1, nodes = copyNodesStoch, logProbOnly = TRUE)
                } else {
                    nimCopy(from = mvSaved, to = model, row = 1, nodes = calcNodesProposalStage, logProb = TRUE)
                    nimCopy(from = mvSaved, to = model, row = 1, nodes = copyNodesDeterm, logProb = FALSE)
                    nimCopy(from = mvSaved, to = model, row = 1, nodes = copyNodesStoch, logProbOnly = TRUE)
                }
            }
            if(adaptive)     adaptiveProcedure(jump)
        }
    },
    methods = list(
        generateProposalVector = function() {
            propValueVector <- rmnorm_chol(1, values(model,target), chol_propCov_scale, 0)  ## last argument specifies prec_param = FALSE
            returnType(double(1))
            return(propValueVector)
        },
        adaptiveProcedure = function(jump = logical()) {
            timesRan <<- timesRan + 1
            if(jump)     timesAccepted <<- timesAccepted + 1
            if(!adaptScaleOnly)     empirSamp[timesRan, 1:d] <<- values(model, target)
            if(timesRan %% adaptInterval == 0) {
                acceptanceRate <- timesAccepted / timesRan
                timesAdapted <<- timesAdapted + 1
                if(saveMCMChistory) {
                    setSize(scaleHistory, timesAdapted)                 ## scaleHistory
                    scaleHistory[timesAdapted] <<- scale                ## scaleHistory
                    setSize(acceptanceHistory, timesAdapted)            ## scaleHistory
                    acceptanceHistory[timesAdapted] <<- acceptanceRate  ## scaleHistory
                    propCovTemp <- propCovHistory                                           ## scaleHistory
                    setSize(propCovHistory, timesAdapted, d, d)                             ## scaleHistory
                    if(timesAdapted > 1)                                                    ## scaleHistory
                        for(iTA in 1:(timesAdapted-1))                                      ## scaleHistory
                            propCovHistory[iTA, 1:d, 1:d] <<- propCovTemp[iTA, 1:d, 1:d]    ## scaleHistory
                    propCovHistory[timesAdapted, 1:d, 1:d] <<- propCov[1:d, 1:d]            ## scaleHistory
                }
                adaptFactor <- my_calcAdaptationFactor$run(acceptanceRate)
                scale <<- scale * adaptFactor
                ## calculate empirical covariance, and adapt proposal covariance
                if(!adaptScaleOnly) {
                    gamma1 <- my_calcAdaptationFactor$getGamma1()
                    for(i in 1:d)     empirSamp[, i] <<- empirSamp[, i] - mean(empirSamp[, i])
                    empirCov <- (t(empirSamp) %*% empirSamp) / (timesRan-1)
                    propCov <<- propCov + gamma1 * (empirCov - propCov)
                    chol_propCov <<- chol(propCov)
                }
                chol_propCov_scale <<- chol_propCov * scale
                timesRan <<- 0
                timesAccepted <<- 0
            }
        },
        setScale = function(newScale = double()) {
            scale         <<- newScale
            scaleOriginal <<- newScale
            chol_propCov_scale <<- chol_propCov * scale
        },
        setPropCov = function(newPropCov = double(2)) {
            propCov         <<- newPropCov
            propCovOriginal <<- newPropCov
            chol_propCov <<- chol(propCov)
            chol_propCov_scale <<- chol_propCov * scale
        },
        getScaleHistory = function() {  ## scaleHistory
            if(!saveMCMChistory)   print("Please set 'nimbleOptions(MCMCsaveHistory = TRUE)' before building the MCMC.")
            returnType(double(1))
            return(scaleHistory)
        },
        getAcceptanceHistory = function() {  ## scaleHistory
            returnType(double(1))
            if(!saveMCMChistory)   print("Please set 'nimbleOptions(MCMCsaveHistory = TRUE)' before building the MCMC.")
            return(acceptanceHistory)
        },
        getPropCovHistory = function() { ## scaleHistory
            if(!saveMCMChistory)   print("Please set 'nimbleOptions(MCMCsaveHistory = TRUE)' before building the MCMC and note that to reduce memory use we only save the proposal covariance history for parameter vectors of length infinity or less.")
            returnType(double(3))
            return(propCovHistory)
        },
        reset = function() {
            scale   <<- scaleOriginal
            propCov <<- propCovOriginal
            chol_propCov <<- chol(propCov)
            chol_propCov_scale <<- chol_propCov * scale
            timesRan      <<- 0
            timesAccepted <<- 0
            timesAdapted  <<- 0
            if(saveMCMChistory) {
                scaleHistory  <<- c(0, 0)    ## scaleHistory
                acceptanceHistory  <<- c(0, 0)
                propCovHistory <<- nimArray(0, dim = c(2,d,d))
            }
            my_calcAdaptationFactor$reset()
        }
    )
)

On Tue, Jun 20, 2023 at 10:38 PM Quresh Latif <quresh...@birdconservancy.org> wrote:

> OK, thanks. How do we disable the limit of 10 dimensions for saving proposal covariance histories?
>
>
>
> Also, any suggestions on how to go about identifying reasonable proposal covariances? All I can think of doing is running the model for a short bit and then saving the proposal covariances, but then I’m not sure I’m doing anything more than the automated algorithm for determining the covariance. Are there any good references you can suggest that describe approaches for tuning block samplers?
>
>

> Quresh S. Latif
> Research Scientist
> Bird Conservancy of the Rockies
> Phone: (970) 482-1707 ext. 15

>
> https://link.edgepilot.com/s/beffaaaf/yJozoXsWfkaCBH6bINPh0A?u=http://www.birdconservancy.org/

>
>
> From: Daniel Turek <danie...@gmail.com>
> Sent: Tuesday, June 20, 2023 6:45 PM
> To: Quresh Latif <quresh...@birdconservancy.org>
> Cc: nimble-users <nimble...@googlegroups.com>
> Subject: Re: Improving MCMC convergence
>
>
>
> Quresh, thanks for the message, and it's great that you're digging into these aspects of the samplers.  Just a few comments.
>
>
>
> You could easily work around the limit of 10 dimensions (parameters) for saved proposal covariance histories from the RW_block sampler, and have this history be saved for larger groups of parameters if you wish.  Just be aware of how the memory usage would scale, as d*d*nAdapt, where d is the dimension of the parameter block, and nAdapt is the number of adaptation phases of the RW_block sampler.
>
>
>
> No, I don't agree that "in most cases it probably won't be all that helpful to look at or tweak the covariances in order to optimize mixing?".  The restriction of saving proposal covariance history only for <= 10 dimensional blocks is only for memory-related concerns.  And it's true that the RW_block sampler will likely not operate with any practical efficiency (that is: it will have very low acceptance rate) when *all* of the following are true: (i) operating in high dimensions, (ii) the dimensions are on quite different scales and/or exhibit high correlations between dimensions, and (iii) you do not provide an accurate and informative starting value for the proposal covariance.  However, this situation can be avoided by provided a reasonably accurate starting value for the proposal covariance, and I would also suggest using a small initial "scale" value (subject to tuning, but certainly less than 1).  You can also further encourage efficiency of the RW_block sampler using the "tries" argument, by providing an integer value greater than 1, which will afford the sampler multiple propose-accept/reject cycles for each MCMC iteration.  Following these suggestions, the RW_block sampler could in theory operate quite well even in high dimensions - while being less computationally expensive than the AFSS sampler.  All that said, joint sampling in high dimensional space is generally a difficult problem.
>
>
>
> Regarding the final part of your question: no, even if all dimensions are scaled similarly, for high dimensional sampling it will still be extremely helpful to provide an informative (and accurate) starting value for the proposal covariance, assuming there's nontrivial correlation between the various dimensions.
>
>
>
> I hope this helps.  Cheers,
>
> Daniel
>
>
>
>
>
>
>
>
>
> On Tue, Jun 20, 2023 at 12:04 AM Quresh Latif <quresh...@birdconservancy.org> wrote:
> >
> > I was able to get the proposal covariance history for your example model, but when I try it for my model, I get the following message:
> >
> >
> >
> > "Please set 'nimbleOptions(MCMCsaveHistory = TRUE)' before building the MCMC and note that to reduce memory use we only save the proposal covariance history for parameter vectors of length 10 or less."
> >
> > I did set 'nimbleOptions(MCMCsaveHistory = TRUE)', but many of my blocks include more than 10 parameters. It looks like (as suggested by the message) I am getting covariances saved for blocks of <10 parameters but not for those >10 parameters. I also see a message when setting the block samplers "[Note] Assigning an RW_block sampler to nodes with very different scales can result in low MCMC efficiency. If all nodes assigned to RW_block are not on a similar scale, we recommend providing an informed value for the "propCov" control list argument, or using the AFSS sampler instead.".
> >
> >
> >
> > Taken these messages together, I am getting the sense that in most cases it probably won't be all that helpful to look at or tweak the covariances in order to optimize mixing? Does it normally make sense to just focus on the scale parameter and not worry about the covariances when trying to customize the tuning parameters to speed up mixing (assuming all the parameters in a block are scaled similarly)?
> >
> >
> >
> > On Thursday, June 8, 2023 at 2:24:43 PM UTC-6 Daniel Turek wrote:
> > >
> > > Great questions, Quresh, and I'm glad you're exploring some of the functionality provided with nimble's suite of samplers.  Let me try to address your questions, but please tell me if anything is unclear or you have follow up questions.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > For RW_block samplers, the (scalar) 'scale' and the (matrix) 'propCov' tuning parameters are used together to generate new MH proposals.  Specifically, length-n proposal vectors are generated as MVN(0, cov = Sigma), where Sigma = propCov * scale^2, where Sigma is covariance matrix used to generate the proposed transitions.  During the course of MCMC sampling, the 'propCov' matrix adapts towards the empirical covariance of the posterior samples (which is used to approximate the true covariance of the target dimensions of the posterior distribution).  The 'scale' variable adapts independently, in order to achieve the (theoretically) optimal acceptance rate for the RW_block sampler.  If the acceptance rate is too low, for example, then the 'scale' value will adaptively decrease, to generate smaller (closer to the origin in R^n) proposal vectors, which are more likely to be accepted.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > 2. In that example, the 'scale' could just as well be set also.  But, in the example, we provide an informed initial value for the 'propCov' matrix, then rely on the automatic adaptation of the 'scale' variable.  There is no good reason that the 'scale' was not set, as well.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > 2b. If by "fix the tuning" you mean set the sampler tuning parameters to immutable values, then you should also set adaptive = FALSE (in addition to providing values for 'propCov' and 'scale').  If you want to provide a fixed covariance structure for proposals, but allow 'scale' to self-adapt to achieve the (theoretically) optimal acceptance rate, then you should set adaptScaleOnly = TRUE (in addition to providing a value for 'propCov').  Alternatively, you can allow these variables to adapt on their own (leaving the default values of adaptive = TRUE and adaptScaleOnly = FALSE), while also providing starting values for 'propCov' and/or 'scale', as you desire.  Nimble is here to meet your needs.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > 3. No, assigning two samplers (say A and B) to the same parameter (say, theta) does not operate as two chains.  It's one chain, where the chain is generated as:
> > >
> > > (a) sampler A acts on theta, and may modify the value of theta
> > >
> > > (b) sampler B acts on theta, and may further modify the value of theta
> > >
> > > (c) record the current value of theta as the next value in the (single) chain of samples
> > >
> > > (d) goto (a) above
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > To see all the samplers that are operating, printed in the order in which they'll operate, between each successive sample that is recorded, don't forget about our old friend:
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > conf$printSamplers()
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Cheers,
> > >
> > > Daniel
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > On Thu, Jun 8, 2023 at 2:45 PM Quresh Latif <quresh...@birdconservancy.org> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > I was able to recover tuning histories for my large model with a mix of RW and RW_block samplers. My co-worker and I were reviewing the vignette <https://link.edgepilot.com/s/6d6c1ee4/i7DIuUarSkqzXlUpiCfKdA?u=http://danielturek.github.io/public/RWscaleHistory/RWscaleHistory.html> referred to earlier in this thread, and we came up with some questions that might be relevant to anyone interested in specifying samplers with customized tuning:
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > 1. For RW_block samplers, how is scale related to covariance matrix, or are they related at all, or conversely how do they operate together to determine jump probabilities?
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > 2. For the example in the vignette, why isn't scale set along with covariance matrix for the block sampler in this line?

> > > > > > > > > > Sometimes the list of samplers operating on a model represents misplaced computational costs.  A categorical sampler for a node with many categories can be inefficient, and that node may not be a limitation on mixing, so it can work well to use a faster sampler.  Sometimes multiple nodes share identical or nearly identical dependencies (other nodes that depend on them).  This means that the same computational effort is involved in sampling them, and for this reason it can make sense to sample them jointly, such as with RW_block.  Sometimes we can identify parts of a model that can be re-written using nimbleFunctions to provide new functions or distributions in the model.  New functions can combine multiple steps into single steps, reducing the size of the model, which can improve efficiency.  New distributions can be useful to analytically sum or integrate over latent states when it is simple to do so.  The zero-inflated Poisson example on our web site is a simple case.  More complicated cases of doing this for capture-recapture and hidden Markov models are given in Turek et al. (2016; Environ Ecol Stat (2016) 23: 549. https://link.edgepilot.com/s/53661c95/X7avF18thkyInmDB4XXrbA?u=https://doi.org/10.1007/s10651-016-0353-z). messages.subject: Assistance with Parallelizing the "modparcov" Function for Improved Execution Time
messages.subject_clean: Assistance with Parallelizing the "modparcov" Function for Improved Execution Time
messages.body_plain:
Hi

I hope this email finds you well. I am writing to seek your expertise and assistance with a programming challenge I am currently facing.
I have developed a function called "modparcov," which is crucial for my program's convergence. However, the execution time of this function
is significantly long, and I would like to optimize it for improved performance.
To address this issue, I have decided to run the program on a server with more than 20 cores. My intention is to parallelize the "modparcov" function,
allowing it to run concurrently and take advantage of the server's multiple cores. However, I am in need of guidance to achieve this parallelization effectively.

I would greatly appreciate it if you could provide assistance and guidance on how to parallelize the "modparcov" function. Specifically,
I am seeking advice on how to modify the code to ensure efficient utilization of the available cores and improve the overall execution time of my program.

If you have any suggestions, recommendations, or sample code snippets that demonstrate how to parallelize such functions effectively, please do share them
with me. Additionally, if there are any best practices or resources you could recommend for optimizing code execution through parallelization, I would be extremely grateful.
Thank you in advance for your time and assistance.
Your expertise and guidance will be of immense help in enhancing the performance of my program. I look forward to hearing from you soon.

Warm regards

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

library(spdep)
library(nimble)
library(GWmodel)

N <- S <- 211

data("baltimore")

y <- baltimore$PRICE

y <- matrix(y, nrow = length(y), ncol = length(y), byrow = FALSE)

x <- cbind(baltimore$DWELL,baltimore$NBATH,baltimore$PATIO,baltimore$FIREPL,
           baltimore$AC,baltimore$BMENT,baltimore$GAR,baltimore$CITCOU,baltimore$LOTSZ)

coords <- cbind(baltimore$X,baltimore$Y)

dist2 <- gw.dist(coords,focus=0,p=2,theta=0,longlat=F)

bw <- bw.gwr(PRICE~DWELL+NBATH+PATIO+FIREPL+AC+BMENT+GAR+CITCOU+LOTSZ,
             data=SpatialPointsDataFrame(coords,baltimore),approach="AIC",kernel="gaussian",
             adaptive=T,p=2,theta=0,longlat=F,dMat=dist2)

modparcov <- function(y, x, w) {

  # Main Function
  GWRCode <- nimbleCode({
    for (i in 1:S) {
      y[1:N, i] ~ dmnorm(mu_y[1:N, i], prec = tau_y0[1:N, 1:N, i])

      mu_y[1:N, i] <- b[i, 1] * x[, 1] + b[i, 2] * x[, 2] + b[i, 3] *
        x[, 3] + b[i, 4] * x[, 4] + b[i, 5] * x[, 5] + b[i, 6] * x[, 6] +
        b[i, 7] * x[, 7] + b[i, 8] * x[, 8] + b[i, 9] * x[, 9]

      tau_y0[1:N, 1:N, i] <- diag(psi_y[i] * exp(-Dist[1:N, i] / lambda))

      for (j in 1:9) {
        b[i, j] ~ dnorm(0, tau = tau_b[ind[j] + 1])
        ind[j] ~ dbern(gamma[j])
        tau_b[1] <- tau_b0
        tau_b[2] <- tau_b0 * c
        gamma[j] ~ dbeta(0.5, 0.5)
      }

      b0[i] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
      psi_y[i] ~ dgamma(1, 1)
    }
    lambda ~ dunif(0, D)
  })

  GWRData <- list(y = y, Dist = dist2, x = x)
  GWRConst <- list(S = S, N = N, D = 50, tau_b0 = 100, c = 0.0001)
  GWRInits <- list(psi_y = rep(1, GWRConst$S), ind = c(rep(1, 9)),
                   gamma = rep(0.5, 9), lambda = 10)

  # Run the Model

  beta <- as.matrix(colMeans(matrix((pos_mcmc[, 1:1899]), N , 9)))

  sigma_y <- 1 / (mean(pos_mcmc[, 1900]))

  xpw <- t(x) %*% w
  invxpwx <- solve(xpw %*% x)
  c <- invxpwx %*% xpw

  res$cov <- ccp * as.numeric(varresid)
  res

Scott, it's great that you're writing your own package containing nimbleFunctions, and I'm certain there's a way to make it work as you're imagining.  That said, from reviewing this information I'm not immediately sure what the issue is.

For other examples of packages providing nimbleFunctions, you can also take a look at nimbleSCR <https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimbleSCR>, nimbleHMC <https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimbleHMC>, and nimbleSMC <https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimbleSMC>.

Beyond this suggestion, we might need to really look at your actual package code to figure out what the issue is.

Cheers,
Daniel

messages.subject: Re: support for sparse matrices?
messages.body_plain:
Scott, briefly -- no, at present there is no native support for sparse matrix operations in nimble.  This is a goal of current development work, but be aware it's a long-term effort.

In order to interface with other existing sparse matrix C libraries, the nimbleExternalCall functionality might be what you're looking for.  This provides access to other (existing, compiled) C++ functions from inside nimbleFunctions.  See help(nimbleExternalCall) for more information and an example.  Fundamentally, you'll need the header (*.h) file and the compiled (*.o) object file.  With those in hand, you should be able to access the routines you're after from inside nimbleFunctions.

Let me know if this helps get you started in the right direction.

Cheers,
Daniel

messages.subject: Re: Missing value in response
messages.body_plain:
Duoduo, thanks for your question.  Missing (NA) values in the response will generally be handled fine.  One exception is if you have a partially-observed response vector following a multivariate distribution (for example, a multivariate normal likelihood distribution, where only some elements of the response vector are observed and some are NA), in which case special care might be necessary.  But, if your response data are scalar observations (each following a univariate distribution), then the MCMC will handle these missing (NA) values with posterior predictive samplers.

If you want to avoid issues of logProb being -Inf, you can try providing values for the missing observations using the initial values list when building the model.

If one of your MCMC samplers is repeatedly issuing warnings about logProbs being -Inf, on every MCMC iteration, then something might be going wrong.

Cheers,
Daniel

messages.subject: Re: Dynamic indexing found in a vector of indices
messages.subject_clean: Dynamic indexing found in a vector of indices
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dongchen,

I think you'll want to calculate start and end vectors of length 39 in regular R code outside of the NIMBLE model, then provide them to the nimbleModel function in the "constants" list when you build it. You'll then be able to reference X.mod[start[i]:end[i]] for each i in your loop.

NIMBLE uses declarative code to define a network of related nodes at build time. Anything that defines an index--such as start and end in your model, or something like the length of a for-loop--needs to be provided at build time as a "constant" and it can't be modified once the model is built. Also because it's declarative, unlike R, NIMBLE won't loop through and redefine "start" and "end" parameters iteratively--you can only define a given variable once in a NIMBLE model.

Hope this helps--
Ben

messages.body_plain:
Dongchen, it's difficult to diagnose without actually running (and inspecting) the model and the MCMC, but is it possible that the first element X.mod[1] is unconstrained?  That is, start[i] > 1 for all i, and thus X.mod[1] has no dependencies?  That could be an explanation for what you're seeing, where the sampling appears to be unconstrained.

Beyond that, it would also help to know what MCMC samplers you have operating.  If you have the default RW_block sampler operating in 156-dimensional space on the entirety of X.mod[1:156], then I would not expect it to work well in any case, although I would not guess in the manner that you're seeing.  I might suggest also trying the elliptical slice sampler ("ess" sampler), which is specialized for sampling multivariate normal distributions as you have for X.mod[1:156].  Otherwise, what you're observing must in some way reflect the model structure, the observations, and the samplers you have operating.

I hope this helps, good luck,
Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Hi, could you say more about what specific part of the computation you're trying to parallelize?

If you're trying to run multiple chains in parallel, we have information in this example on our website <https://r-nimble.org/nimbleExamples/parallelizing_NIMBLE.html>.

Also, one comment about efficiency: because your precision matrix, `tau_y0`, is diagonal, it's likely to be more efficient to just
define the elements of `y[1:N, i]` as scalar nodes following the `dnorm` distribution with the appropriate scalar precision.
This will avoid unnecessary matrix computations in computing the likelihood for `y`.

-Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Gesa,

I'm just looking at this now -- sorry that none of us could take a look sooner.

I'm having trouble reproducing the behavior you are seeing when I slightly modify your code as seen below to build and compile the model.

```
  myModel <- nimbleModel(code=myCode,
                         constants=data,
                         inits=inits()
                         calculate=FALSE)

  CmyModel <- compileNimble(myModel)
```

When I build the model with `nimbleModel` it takes something like 5 minutes and uses about 4 GB of memory. Then compiling the model with `compileNimble` takes about a minute and memory use stays at about 4 GB.
I could imagine that if your machine is slower than mine, the times might be somewhat longer, but I'd be surprised if it were more than 20-30 minutes given the timing I am seeing.

Are you on a machine with limited memory? If so, it's possible that you're using up all the memory on your machine and everything slows to a crawl because the operating system is swapping (using disk in place of memory, which is much, much slower). If your machine has less than, say, 10 GB memory, I suggest you try to monitor memory and CPU usage and see if memory use gets up to the maximum physical memory on the machine and CPU usage drops way below 100%).

-chris

From: Gesa von Hirschheydt <g.v.hir...@gmail.com>
Date: Sun, Jun 11, 2023 at 6:57 AM
Subject: Two-season multi-species occupancy model does not compile with large data set
To: <nimble...@googlegroups.com>

Dear NIMBLE users

I have recently switched to NIMBLE from JAGS, because I hoped it could reduce the eternal run time (> 10 days for 1000 iterations) I am experiencing in JAGS when trying to fit a two-season multi-species occupancy model to my data.

The data come from a standardized community survey of epiphytic lichens across Switzerland. The goal of the analysis is to estimate the relative change in occupancy of each species between the two seasons. Here some details on data structure:

·       2 “seasons” (20 years ago, and now)

·       733 sites (313 were surveyed in both seasons, 328 only in season 1, 92 only in season 2; 270 of all sites never had any detection at all, because there is no substrate for epiphytic lichens on these sites)

·       334 species (only 60 of these have detections at > 25 sites, very many species are observed only once or twice)

·       within each season, only 46 sites have a repeated visit (i.e., the number of visits per season is 1 for most sites, and 2 for 46 sites)

·       11 observers

The model I am trying to fit is a 2-season multi-species occupancy model (model.R attached). I opted for a 2-season model rather than a dynamic model to limit the number of parameters, and because not all sites were surveyed in two seasons. Here some details on the model:

·       intercept for occupancy with a random effect for species

·       5 covariates for occupancy (each with random effect for species)

·       observer-specific intercepts for detection (each with a random effect for species)

·       3 covariates for detection (as these covariates are species- or survey-specific, there is no need for a random effect for species here)

The data are in array format (y[i,j,t,k] for site i, visit j, season t, and species k), but I use indices in the for-loops so that for each site, the model only “looks at” (or iterates through) the seasons during which this site was surveyed and only at the number of visits (1 or 2) that were actually made.

This model runs fine when I fit it to a reduced data set (60 most common species and using only the 463 sites that had at least 1 epiphytic lichen; 0_data.RData attached). However, the model does not even want to compile within 3 days when I use the full dataset (1_data.RData attached).

I have tried to find ways to speed up the compilation process, and have applied the two tricks suggested by Olivier Gimenez in his book (https://oliviergimenez.github.io/banana-book/intronimble.html#tips-and-tricks). I also considered integrating over the latent state, because Ponisio et al. 2020 (https://doi.org/10.1002/ece3.6053) showed that this slightly improved efficiency of MCMC sampling in multi-season multi-species occupancy models, but as I want to know the proportion of occupied sites per species and season, I need the latent state variable z to sum over. This same paper also said that the default samplers of NIMBLE were the most efficient in comparison to alternative (manually defined) samplers, switching sampler does therefore not seem a promising option.

So I have these questions: Why does this model not want to compile? Is there anything I can do to speed up the compilation and (if necessary once the model is compiled) the running of the MCMC chains?

I know that the data set is quite large with so many (rare) species and so many (empty) sites, and I could just slice the data into pieces (e.g., single-season model to only a portion of the species using only sites with at least 1 detection), but that wasn’t really the point of assembling this data set… and it would be a pity to not model all species and the two seasons jointly for all the shared parameters. In JAGS, a single-season multi-species occupancy model with similar covariates and fit to the data from the first season only runs and converges well after ca. 4 days. That would thus be my undesirable plan B.

Best wishes

Gesa

messages.subject: Re: Multisite model with m-array
messages.body_plain:
Hi Amélie,

I'm not seeing that the model gets stuck. Instead I see an error occurring when the MCMC is configured that cause MCMC configuration to fail. We've tracked that down to a bug in how nimble checks conjugacy with the complicated structure of how you define `pr`.

We'll fix that in the next release, but for now, please turn off conjugacy checking before running `nimbleMCMC`.

You can do this by setting a nimble option:

nimbleOptions(MCMCuseConjugacy = FALSE)

This shouldn't affect how sampling is done, because conjugate samplers wouldn't be assigned to your model in any case.

If that doesn't address things, let us know. (In particular, it may be that the 'getting stuck' problem is a distinct problem.)

-chris

messages.subject: Re: Two-season multi-species occupancy model does not compile with large data set
messages.subject_clean: Two-season multi-species occupancy model does not compile with large data set
messages.body_plain:
Dear Chris

Thanks for your reply.
I've been using the high-performance cluster of my institute. Together with the parallelized code I shared here, I asked the cluster to use one CPU per chain (5 chains) and I assigned each CPU a memory of 10 GB.

I tried your simplified code and found similar run times for these two functions: 5-7 min for myModel <- nimbleModel(myCode) and 2-3 min for CmyModel <- compileNimble(myModel).
So I tried to run this non-parallelized version on the cluster and it seems to get stuck at the stage right after that:

myMCMC <- buildMCMC(CmyModel, monitors=monitors, useConjugacy=FALSE)

One attempt to run past this function failed after 5 hours, the other after 10 hours, both with the error message OUT-OF-MEMORY despite 10 GB. I am currently trying again with 15 GB.
Fitting the same model with 111 instead of 334 species works perfectly fine, even with 6 GB/CPU. It compiles, runs, and converges after 4-6 hours. Is it just the large number of nodes that makes the full model get stuck or should I substantially increase the GB/CPU and reduce the number of chains?

Best wishes
Gesa

Am Mi., 28. Juni 2023 um 19:53 Uhr schrieb Chris Paciorek <paci...@stat.berkeley.edu>:
> Hi Gesa,
>
> I'm just looking at this now -- sorry that none of us could take a look sooner.
>
> I'm having trouble reproducing the behavior you are seeing when I slightly modify your code as seen below to build and compile the model.
>
> ```
>   myModel <- nimbleModel(code=myCode,
>                          constants=data,
>                          inits=inits()
>                          calculate=FALSE)
>
>   CmyModel <- compileNimble(myModel)
> ```
>
> When I build the model with `nimbleModel` it takes something like 5 minutes and uses about 4 GB of memory. Then compiling the model with `compileNimble` takes about a minute and memory use stays at about 4 GB.
> I could imagine that if your machine is slower than mine, the times might be somewhat longer, but I'd be surprised if it were more than 20-30 minutes given the timing I am seeing.
>
> Are you on a machine with limited memory? If so, it's possible that you're using up all the memory on your machine and everything slows to a crawl because the operating system is swapping (using disk in place of memory, which is much, much slower). If your machine has less than, say, 10 GB memory, I suggest you try to monitor memory and CPU usage and see if memory use gets up to the maximum physical memory on the machine and CPU usage drops way below 100%).
>
> -chris
>
> ---------- Forwarded message ---------
> From: Gesa von Hirschheydt <g.v.hir...@gmail.com>
> Date: Sun, Jun 11, 2023 at 6:57 AM
> Subject: Two-season multi-species occupancy model does not compile with large data set
> To: <nimble...@googlegroups.com>
>
>
> Dear NIMBLE users
>
>
>
> I have recently switched to NIMBLE from JAGS, because I hoped it could reduce the eternal run time (> 10 days for 1000 iterations) I am experiencing in JAGS when trying to fit a two-season multi-species occupancy model to my data.
>
>
>
> The data come from a standardized community survey of epiphytic lichens across Switzerland. The goal of the analysis is to estimate the relative change in occupancy of each species between the two seasons. Here some details on data structure:
>
> ·       2 “seasons” (20 years ago, and now)
>
> ·       733 sites (313 were surveyed in both seasons, 328 only in season 1, 92 only in season 2; 270 of all sites never had any detection at all, because there is no substrate for epiphytic lichens on these sites)
>
> ·       334 species (only 60 of these have detections at > 25 sites, very many species are observed only once or twice)
>
> ·       within each season, only 46 sites have a repeated visit (i.e., the number of visits per season is 1 for most sites, and 2 for 46 sites)
>
> ·       11 observers
>
>
>
> The model I am trying to fit is a 2-season multi-species occupancy model (model.R attached). I opted for a 2-season model rather than a dynamic model to limit the number of parameters, and because not all sites were surveyed in two seasons. Here some details on the model:
>
> ·       intercept for occupancy with a random effect for species
>
> ·       5 covariates for occupancy (each with random effect for species)
>
> ·       observer-specific intercepts for detection (each with a random effect for species)
>
> ·       3 covariates for detection (as these covariates are species- or survey-specific, there is no need for a random effect for species here)
>
>
>
> The data are in array format (y[i,j,t,k] for site i, visit j, season t, and species k), but I use indices in the for-loops so that for each site, the model only “looks at” (or iterates through) the seasons during which this site was surveyed and only at the number of visits (1 or 2) that were actually made.
>
>
>
> This model runs fine when I fit it to a reduced data set (60 most common species and using only the 463 sites that had at least 1 epiphytic lichen; 0_data.RData attached). However, the model does not even want to compile within 3 days when I use the full dataset (1_data.RData attached).
>
>
>
> I have tried to find ways to speed up the compilation process, and have applied the two tricks suggested by Olivier Gimenez in his book (https://oliviergimenez.github.io/banana-book/intronimble.html#tips-and-tricks). I also considered integrating over the latent state, because Ponisio et al. 2020 (https://doi.org/10.1002/ece3.6053) showed that this slightly improved efficiency of MCMC sampling in multi-season multi-species occupancy models, but as I want to know the proportion of occupied sites per species and season, I need the latent state variable z to sum over. This same paper also said that the default samplers of NIMBLE were the most efficient in comparison to alternative (manually defined) samplers, switching sampler does therefore not seem a promising option.
>
>
>
> So I have these questions: Why does this model not want to compile? Is there anything I can do to speed up the compilation and (if necessary once the model is compiled) the running of the MCMC chains?
>
>
>
> I know that the data set is quite large with so many (rare) species and so many (empty) sites, and I could just slice the data into pieces (e.g., single-season model to only a portion of the species using only sites with at least 1 detection), but that wasn’t really the point of assembling this data set… and it would be a pity to not model all species and the two seasons jointly for all the shared parameters. In JAGS, a single-season multi-species occupancy model with similar covariates and fit to the data from the first season only runs and converges well after ca. 4 days. That would thus be my undesirable plan B.
>
>
>
> Best wishes
>
> Gesa

Hi Chris,
Thank you so much for your help.

Since I couldn't find a solution using the dirichlet distribution in the model (probably due to the configuration of the MCMCs as you've just explained, but to be honest I wouldn't have been able to find this issue).
I coded myself to obtain dirichlet distributions using gamma distributions:

    for(i in 1:ns){
      lpsi1[i] ~ dgamma(1,1)
      lpsi2[i] ~ dgamma(1,1)
      lpsi3[i] ~ dgamma(1,1)
      lpsi4[i] ~ dgamma(1,1)
      lpsi5[i] ~ dgamma(1,1)
    }
    psi1[1:ns] <- lpsi1[1:ns]/sum(lpsi1[1:ns])
    psi2[1:ns] <- lpsi2[1:ns]/sum(lpsi2[1:ns])
    psi3[1:ns] <- lpsi3[1:ns]/sum(lpsi3[1:ns])
    psi4[1:ns] <- lpsi4[1:ns]/sum(lpsi4[1:ns])
    psi5[1:ns] <- lpsi5[1:ns]/sum(lpsi5[1:ns])

With this method, the models run smoothly.
Does this sound right to you?
That way seems correct for you also?
Thanks again for your time and solution !
Amélie

I am a beginner in Nimble. I did a few models but I am facing an error now. I hope you can help me to solve it.
I am doing a CJS model with multiple states and there also exists uncertainties in assigning states. I attached my R code here and also a trial data which I am using to test my model.
The model was running without any problem until I incorporated more states. The initial error I am getting is
[Note] Infinite values were detected in model variables: logProb_alive, logProb_mydata.
And, then after compiling I am also getting a lot of lines of error,
.....
warning: problem initializing stochastic node alive[1, 2]: logProb is -Inf. warning: problem initializing stochastic node alive[2, 2]: logProb is -Inf. warning: problem initializing stochastic node alive[5, 7]: logProb is -Inf. warning: problem initializing stochastic node alive[7, 6]: logProb is -Inf. warning: problem initializing stochastic node alive[9, 2]: logProb is -Inf. warning: logProb of data node mydata[3, 1]: logProb is -Inf. warning: logProb of data node mydata[4, 2]: logProb is -Inf. warning: logProb of data node mydata[9, 1]: logProb is -Inf. warning: problem initializing stochastic node alive[4, 4]: logProb is -Inf. warning: problem initializing stochastic node alive[8, 4]: logProb is -Inf. warning: problem initializing stochastic node alive[1, 4]: logProb is -Inf. warning: logProb of data node mydata[2, 3]: logProb is -Inf.
.......
I thought the problem was arising from initializing, so I tried different ways. But, I am still getting the same errors. It would be great if anyone has any ideas on how can I fix this problem or if I am doing any mistakes in my code.
